accuracy.evidence: Checked against the NC Year 5 Forces statutory wording (mechanisms including levers, pulleys and gears allow a smaller force to have a greater effect), BBC Bitesize KS2/KS3 moments, and the standard ideal-machine relations. Lever: effort × effort arm = load × load arm, so a load of 6 at 2 spaces is balanced by a push of 3 at 4 spaces (3×4=6×2) and by 12/d in the lab. Fixed pulley: changes direction only; effort ≈ load. Two supporting strands: effort ≈ load/2 and twice the rope (8 shared → pull 4). Gears: 8 teeth driving 16 teeth means half the turns and about twice the turning force. Work = force × distance is conserved on all three cards (3×4=6×2, 4×2=8×1, 2×1=1×2). Parameter corners: p3 a/2 for 8,12,16; p4 w/2 for 16,24,32; m4 n/2 for even n in 2–6.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented KS2 errors (NCETM Year 5 forces; common Bitesize pitfalls): sitting closer to the pivot to make a see-saw easier; thinking any pulley halves the force (a single fixed flagpole pulley does not); believing a machine gives extra energy so a smaller force can also act over a shorter distance; mixing bicycle gears (thinking a high gear is easier uphill); expecting a small gear to make a large gear faster and stronger at once. Each appears as a prediction option, setD/lift/setStrands/spin feedback, or a challenge tag (closer, fixed, free, gear).

lab_distinct.evidence: flaglever has three different mechanisms on one canvas: a see-saw whose rider can be dragged along effort-arm marks with a live 'push needed' readout, a flagpole whose rope must be pulled down to raise a flag (force unchanged), a one-vs-two-strand pulley comparison (8 vs 4, twice the rope), meshed 8- and 16-tooth gears that rotate in opposite directions, and a work-matching table. flagdrop and flagramp treat falling and rolling, not pivots, rope strands or gear teeth, so this lab cannot be reused for those topics by renaming labels.

lab_teaches.evidence: Moving the rider updates 'Push needed' immediately (12/d), so the child sees the force fall as the effort arm grows before the text says so. Raising the flag by pulling down, with the message that the pull stays about as big as the flag, disproves 'any pulley makes it lighter'. Switching to two pulleys shows 'You pull: 4' and 'but twice the rope' together. Turning the gears prints how far each has rotated (small turns 2.0 → large turns 1.0). The last step lines up the three matching products.

predictions.evidence: Five predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab then disproves: sit 'closer to the middle' or 'on the pivot' to lift with less push; a flagpole pulley 'cuts the force in half' or makes the flag lose mass; two pulleys mean 'pull 4 and half the rope' or 'pull 16'; a small gear makes the large one 'faster, with less force' or 'same speed plus free extra force'; and a smaller force means 'extra energy for nothing' or 'the load itself gets lighter'. reveal() names their pick and the right answer.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven rotating questions (effort arm, fixed pulley, shared-load catch, gear trade-off, bicycle low gear, the 6-at-2 / sit-at-4 calculation of 3, and why force and distance trade). Each wrong choice has its own tag and message: closer (nearer the pivot makes you push harder), fixed (direction changes, weight does not), free (no extra energy; longer distance), gear (low gear trades speed for an easier push). Answer order rotates each turn.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation FK combined 2.6 (paragraphs 1.8 to 3.9), adult combined 6.7 (paragraphs 4.6 to 8.3), keyIdea 4.8; family limits 5.0 kid and 10.0 adult. The curriculum words pivot, load, effort, lever, pulley, gear, turning force and low gear are each used with their meaning. Sentences stay short, and the work idea is written as 'a smaller force always acts over a longer distance'.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one mechanism (lever and pivot; see-saw seating; fixed vs sharing pulleys; gears and the force–distance trade). The adult text gives the Year 5 Forces link, the three ideal-machine relations, four named mistakes and what each lab step does. No filler phrase matched.

mobile.evidence: The see-saw unit width is min(52,(W−40)/10), so six effort marks fit at 390 px. The flagpole, pulley pair and two gears are centred and scale with W and H. Every action has a button with min-height 48 px under the canvas (Closer/Farther, Pull down, One pulley/Two pulleys, driver choice, Turn). Feedback wraps to two lines. Work-matching cards stack in three rows rather than requiring a wide table.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas drag has a button twin: move the rider, pull the flag rope, switch one vs two pulleys, choose which gear drives, and turn the gears. The see-saw plank, flag rope and gears also accept pointer drags. The canvas aria-label and live region update on every piece of feedback. Challenge answers sit in a labelled group with a polite live region. Fills mix theme tokens into C.pn so the plank, box, rider, flag and gears keep contrast in both light and dark.

sources: National Curriculum in England: science programmes of study, Year 5 Forces — mechanisms including levers, pulleys and gears (DfE, 2013)

NCETM / primary science guidance on Year 5 forces and simple machines
